name: Echo Question
pattern: Question[echo] applied to Host:Clause[clause type preserved] / Non-headed clausal-semantics construction + echo prosody (+ variable phrase in situ)

entry.name: Echo Question
entry.pattern: Question[echo] applied to Host:Clause[clause type preserved] / Non-headed clausal-semantics construction + echo prosody (+ variable phrase in situ)

dimensions.form: An independently typed Clause or licensed clause-analogue construction echoes a prior utterance, often with rising or rise-fall prosody; a questioned constituent may be replaced by an in-situ variable phrase
dimensions.meaning: Questions what the previous speaker said or meant, rather than directly questioning the echoed proposition
dimensions.function: Requests repetition or clarification of a prior utterance, often also conveying surprise or incredulity
dimensions.distribution: Response to a linguistic stimulus; overlays declarative, closed-interrogative, imperative, and other Clause types without replacing them, and also licenses non-headed echo hosts

1.definition: Repeats all or part of a prior utterance to ask whether that is what the previous speaker said
1.details: The echo question is not a sixth clause type. Question is a semantic category applied as a stimulus-dependent layer while a clausal host preserves its grammatical type and a non-headed host remains non-headed. Its implicit propositional content concerns the prior speech act: an echo of Is he resigning? asks approximately whether the previous speaker asked that question, not whether he is resigning (CGEL pp. 853–54, 886–90).

examples.form: A: She is leaving on Saturday. B: [She is leaving on Saturday]?
examples.note: Repetition echo with declarative clause type preserved

examples.form: A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
examples.note: The echo remains a closed interrogative Clause

examples.form: A: Ed is quite competent. B: [Ed quite competent]?
examples.note: Bare-predication echo with a non-headed host; question semantics does not make it a Clause

2.definition: Replaces a poorly heard or understood part of the stimulus with an in-situ variable phrase to request clarification
2.details: Variable echoes normally retain the word order and clause type of the stimulus rather than acquiring ordinary open-interrogative syntax. Reduction and deictic adjustment are common because the stimulus came from another speaker.

examples.form: A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
examples.note: Variable echo superimposed on an imperative Clause

examples.form: A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?
examples.note: Variable echo superimposed on a closed interrogative Clause, with deictic shift

constraints.description: Requires a recoverable linguistic stimulus whose wording or interpretation is being repeated or clarified.

The echo overlay does not determine syntactic category: an underlying declarative, closed-interrogative, imperative, or other headed Clause retains its defining syntax, and a licensed non-headed host does not become a Clause.
Variable echoes may leave the questioned phrase in the position corresponding to the stimulus and may reduce other recoverable material.

projection.target: Recognizing an echo question predicts preservation of the host's syntactic classification, stimulus-bound deictic adjustment, possible in-situ variable replacement, and answers directed to what was said or meant rather than directly to the echoed proposition
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts echo with ordinary questions through clause-type preservation, stimulus dependence, deictic shift, variable placement, and response interpretation on pp. 853–54 and 886–90

grounds.note: Clause-type preservation, stimulus dependence, and variable placement recur across echo subtypes

diagnostics: response targets what was said or meant

known_boundary_items: Declarative questions such as They've finished? seek confirmation of a proposition using declarative syntax but need not echo a linguistic stimulus.
Ordinary open interrogatives are typed by an interrogative phrase and normally front a non-subject phrase; variable echoes preserve stimulus order.

relatedConstructions.notes: Echo Question specializes Question by making the questioned content a prior linguistic stimulus
Many echoes overlay an independently typed headed Clause without becoming a clause type
A licensed non-headed expression can host echo-question semantics without becoming a Clause
Declarative questions have declarative syntax and confirmation bias but do not require a linguistic stimulus
Variable echoes may contain similar forms but preserve stimulus order rather than instantiating ordinary open-interrogative syntax

grounds.note: Echo questions overlay independently determined clause types and seek repetition or clarification

curious.title: Repeating what someone said as a question
curious.summary: A speaker can repeat all or part of what was just said, in the form of a question, to check it or to ask for clarification.
curious.body:
If someone says She is leaving on Saturday, you can reply She is leaving on Saturday? with a questioning tune. You're asking whether that is what they said. You aren't asking whether she is leaving.

You can also swap a part you didn't hear or understand for a question word. After Give it to Angela, the reply Give it to who? keeps the original order and asks about the missing piece. The echo depends on what the other person just said.

examples.text: A: She is leaving on Saturday. B: [She is leaving on Saturday]?
A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?

curious.try: Next time you didn't catch a word, say back what you heard and swap the missing part for who or what.

teacher.summary: Helps explain echo questions as a layer over a prior utterance that keeps the clause type of what is echoed.
teacher.explain: An echo question repeats all or part of a prior utterance to ask whether that is what the previous speaker said. This dictionary says it isn't a sixth clause type: it's a semantic layer on a stimulus, and the clausal host keeps its grammatical type (declarative, closed interrogative, imperative). A non-headed host stays non-headed, as in Ed quite competent? Echoing Is he resigning? asks approximately whether the previous speaker asked that, not whether he's resigning. A variable echo replaces a poorly heard or understood part with an in-situ variable phrase and keeps the stimulus's word order and clause type, sometimes with reduction and deictic shift (Did I use a what?).
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats the echo question as a stimulus-dependent layer over a host, not as a clause type.

examples.text: A: She is leaving on Saturday. B: [She is leaving on Saturday]?
A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
A: Ed is quite competent. B: [Ed quite competent]?
A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?

contrasts.text: A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
contrasts.note: The echo stays a closed interrogative.

contrasts.text: A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?
contrasts.note: Variable echo with deictic shift (you becomes I).

watch_for: A learner might read the reply Is he going to resign? as asking about his resigning, when it checks what the previous speaker asked.
A learner might expect a variable echo to take ordinary question-word order, though it keeps the stimulus's order.
teacher.activity: Pairs take turns saying a sentence with one word hard to hear. The listener echoes it back, swapping the missed word for who or what, and the speaker repeats the word.

child.hook: What do you say when you didn't hear a word?
child.explain: You can say back what you heard as a question. You can swap the missing word for who or what. Someone says Give it to Angela. You say Give it to who?

examples.text: A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
A: I found a snake. B: [You found a what]?

child.play: Whisper a sentence to a friend and mumble one word. They say it back and swap the mumbled word for who or what.
